utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic. Your

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to finish up one of the topics that we started yesterday before moving on. We were talking about Rugovska Klisura. And if we can have Exhibit 4D439 [Realtime transcript read in error "4D39"] on the screen. I see we might have a bit of a delay getting that, so I'll try and see if I can introduce the exhibit before we have it up on the screen. This will be a combat report of the 3rd Army command dated April the 23rd, 1999, strictly confidential number 26-111. And -- and once we get it up on the screen, I'll direct your attention to section 2.1, which is at the bottom of the first page of the B/C/S original and it's at the bottom of the -- the top of the second page in English. Okay. This should be 4D439. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: English translation was 4D39 -- or at least you've been recorded as saying 4D39.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. 4D439. That's -- that's the -- the exhibit. And there should be -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, again, directing your attention to section 2.1 at the bottom of the first page in B/C/S. According to the text here, you'll see, I think, that units of the Pristina Corps undertake assignments tied to this operation relative to a Odluka decision of the commander and participated in a blockade and sweeps with the MUP. And I believe that you have the indication there that units of the NK, which I take to be the Nis Corps, also participated in this operation. Would this information permit you to conclude that in fact the Odluka for such a joint action, the decision of a joint action, had to have been approved at the level of the 3rd Army command of the VJ, given the inclusion of both the Pristina Corps and Nis Corps units in this action?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect to you, as Defence counsel, I kindly ask the Trial Chamber for permission for me to say to you that you're not right. This sentence, "the units of the Nis Corps and the MUP carried out searches in the area of Presevo and Bojanovac, this is an area outside Kosovo and Metohija. It is 150 kilometres and even more away from the Rugovo gorge. So that is a completely, completely different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what about the first part of my question, sir, where it says there that -- the units of the Pristina Corps focus on --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go back to the first part of question. It is correct that the focus of the engagement of the Pristina Corps was to defend the territorial integrity of the country on the basis of my decision and part of the forces, that is to say, the light infantry battalion, 200, 300 men, as it says here in the first sentence, takes part in the blockade of the area during the search of the terrain in the direction towards Rugovska Klisura. That's the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have the top of the -- the top of the second page in the English. And that's the part I want to focus on now. General, this is still on the first page in the B/C/S; the second -- the second dash mark under 2.1. And do you see there it talks about this being a joint operation mounted by the Pristina Corps and the MUP to search the terrain and break up and destroy the STS in the region of Rugovska Klisura? Does this refresh your recollection as to whether in fact this was an operation that had been planned by the MUP or was this a joint operation involving the MUP and the VJ for which there had been a plan prepared by the appropriate VJ officers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really want to be very accurate before this Trial Chamber. This sentence says that what is underway are a few actions in three or four directions. These are independent actions, including the Rugovska Klisura action. As for these actions, the first sentence provides an explanation that part of the units of the corps is carrying out a blockade during the search and the search is being carried out by the MUP. And I assure you, if you look at the documents of the Prosecution, they have to do with the engagement of the MUP. You will see that from the 4th of April onwards it was the MUP that planned the Rugovska Klisura action. The army was doing its own plans and the MUP is make -- was making its own plans. There is another legitimate activity involved there. These two legitimate forces were there, and then there were army units from Montenegro. So this is the action that I remember. I cannot confirm what you've been trying to say all along, yesterday and today, that it was somebody who was planning these actions for the MUP. I assure you, I don't have here in my bag the Prosecution documents that I'm referring, to but I'm sure of what I'm saying, that in February and in April the MUP planned the engagement of their own forces in Rugovska Klisura, the Rugova gorge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you referring to Prosecution documents which have already featured in the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, yes, that is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, all right, I think I've finished up with Rugovska Klisura. If we can move on. Yesterday we went through the planning process in 19 -- focusing on 1998, as we had a full set of zapovest and Odluka map for that period. And we saw the maps for the Drenica-1. And Mr. Ackerman showed you the map for the Ratis actions. And you indicated that commanders would receive extracts of the map applicable for their units during the operation. Am I correct -- am I also correct that commanders at the brigade level or lower would have to prepare the -- the portion of the map detailing their own units -- assignments -- assignments of units within their zone of responsibility for approval by the superior commanding officer to authorise on their own Odluka map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision-making system in the army, from the operative towards the tactical level, to the brigades and battalions, means that decisions of battalion commanders should also be verified by the brigade commander, just like the decision of the brigade commander is verified by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now -- now, I'd like to move to another topic from 1999. The -- the letter that you wrote on the 24th of May, 1999 relating not only to complaints about MUP re-subordination but also alleged MUP tolerance of criminal activities of its members against the Siptar civilian population, murder, rape, looting, et cetera, at mixed check-points. This is Exhibit P1723, which we will have on the screen eventually, but I don't -- I don't think we need it now. General, last Friday you were asked briefly about this letter during your direct examination by your own counsel. And at transcript page 18045, line 3 to 18047, line 12 you discussed it. And quite frankly, apart from showing 5D376, which was a MUP staff document, you denied as being the bases for these serious allegations in this letter: "I still don't know what these serious allegations are based on, and if the bases for these allegations was in fact verified credible information." Can you please enlighten me on the sources for your allegations in this letter that the MUP had tolerance for criminal activities of its members, including murder, rape, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that this is not a letter of mine. This is a report to the commander of the 3rd Army. The immediate reason for me to report to the commander of the army about this in writing is the oral and written report of the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade that there were problems from the point of view of the lack of re-subordination of MUP units in his zone. That is the central issue of this report. In this context, he also has problems with the clean-up of the terrain, as well as problems in terms of a lack of respect for certain norms of conduct during the war. Quite simply, when I received this report - and its content was rather serious - I could not but inform my superior. I wish to tell the Honourable Trial Chamber that I took certain measures in order to see to what extent the information obtained verbally and in the report was really accurate. I sent a team of operatives consisting of Colonel Stefanovic and Colonel Paprica to see on the spot whether there was a chance of having the re-subordination carried through at all. Secondly, I sent a team to check on the clean-up, sanitization of the terrain, to see whether those allegations were correct as well. And thirdly, I sent my assistant for security to that brigade to check on the spot with the security organs in the brigade but also with the head of the OUP of Glogovac whether indeed there were such problems in terms of conduct on the ground by the police. I can say that a few days later the brigade commander reported to me that better cooperation with the OUP had been established. He did not inform me any more about these incriminations. The chief of security continued working on these tasks. But he did not confirm to me up until the end of the war the allegations from this report. As for clean-up, Dr. Tomasevic was sent to the very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question -- I'm very reluctant to interrupt your evidence, but really this is not dealing with the question. The question is very specific: Could you tell counsel the sources for your allegations in the letter that the MUP had tolerance for criminal activities, including murder, rape -- now, these serious allegations, murder, rape. What's your evidence, is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat. On the basis of the oral and written report of the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade. But I asked for permission to say that I wanted these allegations to be checked, and I made an effort to have that done. That is how I continued answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does that mean there's no evidence that you're aware of to support these allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive, up until the end of the war, verifiable arguments in relation to these allegations that crimes had been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing. I see a potential -- not a translation issue but in English things sound differently. When you say you did not receive up until the war verifiable arguments in relation to these allegations, do you mean to say that you have never received verification of these, up -- even at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say to you that this verification did not end on that day ad hoc. It was customary for military security organs to work together with the MUP organs in charge in these verifications. That is what I wanted to say. And now I am answering in concrete terms that I did not receive any new information that would indicate what had been reported on then and what the report contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And now if we can take a moment to go through some other documents that your counsel examined you on in relation -- in relation to this period of time. There was the control inspection of General Velickovic. I would like to go through that rather briefly. First of all, the exhibit for -- number for this is 3D692, and I would ask you to first see if you can agree with me that this particular document consists of several unconnected concerns in the various numbered paragraphs that were found as part of this control inspection by the team sent by the staff of the Supreme Command and that the concerns relating to the Serbian MUP are in fact concentrated and limited solely to paragraph 11, which can be found at both -- at pages 4 of both the English and the B/C/S original. Can we agree on that general description of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I cannot see what you are referring to on the screen, but I have no reason to disbelieve what you're saying. However, all I can see on the screen is item 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... paragraph 11. Can you agree with me, first of all, that the complaint in the second -- actually, I think it's the third paragraph in the English and also the third paragraph in the B/C/S under paragraph -- the third subparagraph under paragraph 11, that the complaints or concerns about privileged positions of the MUP regarding regular payment of salaries, better uniforms, et cetera, has nothing to do with any alleged criminal behaviour but, rather, is related to dissatisfaction among VJ conscripts and their animosity towards the situation where they weren't being paid for the work that they were doing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept your statement. At least, that's how it's been interpreted, a hostile attitude of members of the army to the police. What this is about was that members of the army, especially the reservists, in relation to the members of the team and the members of the Supreme Command and us commanders, expressed dissatisfaction because they did not have certain entitlements, the ones that other armed forces had defending the country. But this was not animosity towards the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I apologise for using too harsh of a term. Would you agree with me that the dissatisfaction of these certain VJ conscripts at the MUP's status as a full-time paid occupation with benefits prescribed by law led to a mass desertion problem with almost one-half of the manpower of the brigade in question leaving in the middle of the war? Let us say, at the time prior to this control inspection.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you that, first of all, half the brigade deserted, especially not because they did not have the same kind of salaries that the MUP had. This is a problem of such complexity, and I personally participated in dealing with it. This team from the General Staff tried to assist in that brief period of time, but this is a problem that's not for this Court to solve. It's for the army to see what can happen in wartime. All I can say is that this was not a reason for half the brigade, as you say, to desert because of dissatisfaction with their salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a significant portion of that brigade did in fact desert during that time period?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know precisely how many left their positions. I know what they told me, because I spoke to hundreds of them. And if you and the Trial Chamber insist on me explaining this further, I'm willing to do so. But that's a different topic, and I don't want to be reprimanded once again for speaking at too great a length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, simply tell us how many left the positions, which is the question. It's a very easy question to answer if you've got all the details. You don't need all this language to explain why you've actually told us nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 802 members of that brigade left for a while and then returned to their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an easy -- it's an easy job, this, if you just listen to the question and answer it. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your assistance. And so that we can be on the same page, am I correct that the complaints contained in paragraph 11 of this control inspection by General Velickovic and the problems -- the unit that we've been talking about, that is to say, that paragraph 11 actually comes from one source, the 354th Infantry Brigade, the unit we've been talking about with the soldiers that left their positions.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report relates to an inspection by the team from the Supreme Command Staff in at least four units. It doesn't say in this text what you are suggesting in your question, to what unit it refers. If you look at the separate reports accompanying this central report, then you could see that, but I simply cannot reply in the affirmative to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, General, the report of General Velickovic it is clear that there are attachments for the 7th, the 354th, the 125th and 252nd Brigades. Surely during the course of the trial you've had time to review those documents and surely at the time of the controlled inspection you were made aware of the precise complaints and will find that the complaints mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to start back again. I'm told that the first part of my question did not get to the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, the report to General Velickovic is clear that there are -- the -- the report of General Velickovic is clear that the attachments contain reports of the reviews of the four specific brigades, among which is the 354th Infantry Brigade, and I'm sure that in reviewing the documents and in the information that the control provided to you at the time that they were on the ground in Pristina, you are aware of the fact that the bulk of paragraph 11 comes word for word from the review of the 354th Infantry Brigade, a document authored by General Terzic available at 5D436, which we can pull up on the screen, a document from your -- from your Defence. And specifically we can fast-forward to page 4 in the Serbian, where it's the last paragraph, marked number 9, and page 5 in the English, where it is paragraph 9 in brackets. And here we -- we see for the first time in a little bit more detail the complaints about the privileged position of the MUP. And I'll ask you: Would you agree with me, based upon this text, that the-- that the vast concerns in this paragraph 9 actually relate to the dissatisfaction with the so-called privileged position of the MUP relating to the MUP having salaries for work, et cetera, and that there is only one very minor reference in passing about individual MUP members resorting to theft?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a different question from the one you started with. This is becoming an -- a really tangled mess because of the way in which the questions are being posed and the way in which they are being answered. We have to get as precise answers as we can, and to do that requires precise questions. Now, you started off wanting to know if only one brigade was complaining. You've now moved from that, without getting an answer, except that the answer is "no," you haven't explored it any further. I take it you're abandoning that. Or is that still the issue that you're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- well, let me back up again. I guess we'll have to take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, do you have knowledge of the facts that the bulk of paragraph 11 is based upon the -- is based upon the report of the 354th Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because I did not participate in the drafting of this report. I have to answer to -- I have to answer a part of your question. Nobody showed me this report at the end of the inspection, as you suggested. This is a conclusion reached by the inspection of the Supreme Command Staff. I agree that what it says here in item 9 is contained in item 11, but I cannot confirm whether some other unit at that time had these or similar objections or comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for my misconception that you had received a copy of these reports at the time of the inspection. Can I therefore then now direct your attention to the part of 5D436 that was paragraph 9, which I believe is still up on the screen, and ask you to review paragraph 9 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 9, would you agree with me that the text of paragraph 9 seems to follow the text and the concerns listed in paragraph 11 almost to a T, except providing even more detail than was in paragraph 11 of the control inspection by General Velickovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already said that. And even if he -- he was to answer it again, it's adding nothing at all to the information that's going to help us to determine this case. It's there for all to see in black and white. Please move to something controversial on which you need to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have one additional question relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you have information, General, so I'm just going to ask you: Do you have any information based upon any news reports in the news these past three days whether in fact the 354th Infantry Brigade still has members demonstrating in Belgrade trying to seek payment for the time that they spent in Kosovo during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have information via television. I don't know which of these reservists are demanding their rights, but I cannot respond in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you indicated you can -- that you firstly were involved in this -- in trying to resolve this matter. Am I correct that the commander of this unit, and in particular the -- his -- one of his subordinates, were under severe pressure from within the VJ, and in fact there were calls from the 3rd Army for them to be-- for them to be replaced, that the -- that new commanders be put in because of the problems that they were having and the manner they were dealing with those problems relating to the desertion of certain of their members?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct your statement. My personal engagement was in the 7th Infantry Brigade, not in the 354th Infantry Brigade, so that what you are referring to is a report either from the team from the army command or the Supreme Command Staff, but I was not personally involved. If you wish to ask me something about that, please be specific. However, this does not refer to my involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Was there -- was there a plan -- or pardon me. Was there action being contemplated to replace the commander and the chief of staff of the brigade, at the brigade level, relating to the problems that they were having with their men?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to 354th Brigade - you weren't specific in your question, so I can only assume that - and some officers were replaced, not only for that reason but for reasons of implementation of combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. One more document I would like to just briefly review on this -- on this theme is 5D506, which is the -- further down the chain the regular combat report of the commander of the 354th Infantry Brigade. And this is a document that we have seen before in this case, so I'll just ask you briefly: In item -- item number 3, subparagraph (b), the second part of subparagraph (b), it says that the "Redeployed units of the PJP in our unit's zone of responsibility and are not complying with the orders and decisions of the SO Podujevo Crisis Staff." And I would just like to ask of you whether in fact your April 25th, 1999 order on re-subordination mentioned or envisaged the Crisis Staffs having control over MUP units.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a single order of the corps command or in a single order of mine is there even any mention of the possibility that some sort of Crisis Staffs should be in command of the army. I cannot certainly command that someone -- order that someone be in command of the MUP. I beg Their Honours to allow us to read this sentence to the end. The gist is that this is the 27th of April. On the 25th of April, the MUP units were supposed to be re-subordinated. The commander asked me for information as to whom these units are responsible to, because they were not re-subordinated to him in that area. And what he says about their non-implementation of the decisions of the Crisis Staff is not only nonsense, because there's no reason for MUP units to be responsible, but also there were many returnees, so the staff of Podujevo of the municipality and the town issued decisions as to how that population should be assisted. Whether this refers to that or not, I can only speculate. But the MUP was not supposed to carry out decisions issued by some sort of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how do you explain this document? Have you got a -- a commander who doesn't know what he's supposed to be doing? Is that -- is that the explanation? Or doesn't know the situation, the relationship between Crisis Staff and -- and MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I would answer differently. The brigade commander is reporting to me that MUP -- the MUP units are not under his control, and they should be. He's asking for information because he wants to know to whom they are re-subordinated so that certain objections which cannot be seen from this document can be channeled. And there are insufficient elements here for me to speculate any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you -- you take the view that it was reasonable for him to think that the MUP should be answerable to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this sentence, Your Honour, Mr. President, I do not conclude decidedly that the commander believes that the MUP should carry out tasks assigned to them by some Municipal Crisis Staff. But I do know that in that area big, huge efforts were made by the provincial executive council and the police and the army to take care of the civilian population and for everybody to be engaged in this. I have other reports on this subject from the point of view of taking in the civilian population, assisting them, and quite simply I am prepared to focus on answering that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. General Lazarevic, I have no further questions for you. I thank you for your assistance in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to complete it, then, did you respond to the question from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, a team went and I went to -- toward that brigade. That is why I drew your attention to the developments that were to follow. Where there was fuller coordination, in terms of taking in the civilian population. We exhibited at least five documents the other day, what this brigade did and what the medical battalion did together with the MUP. That was the problem. These units were not sufficiently involved on time in taking in this very big number of refugees. That was the essence of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I still don't understand whether you told him that -- that there was no question of the MUP being answerable to the Crisis Staff. Was that ever clarified?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the translation here is like, Mr. President, but I don't think it's unclear to the commander that the MUP should not be answerable to the Crisis Staff. But if the decision was made by the municipality somewhere, like in the village of Metohija, to put up the returnees there, then the municipality asked the army and the police for assistance and to be protected from further attacks. They asked for medical material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, there's a clear question. You need to send us a notice regarding who's responsible for them and who commands over them. Now, that is who is responsible for the PJP and who commands over them. Now, did you answer that and send them a notice?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're asking me -- well, I understood about the first part, of the Crisis Staff, that that's what I was being asked, and now you're asking me about the last part of the sentence. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you -- before you go on, is that not what the whole of these two sentences is about? The first part said: "The PJP are not complying with the orders and decisions of the Crisis Staff." And the second sentence says: "You need to send us a notice regarding who is responsible for them and who commands over them." The two are, on the face of it in English, directly related to each other.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I'm talking to you about the factual situation. You are right when you read what is written here that way, but I am talking to you about a problem that was there because up until the 25th the police units were supposed to be re-subordinated to some brigades. I didn't know which ones either. Nobody ordered me. And up until the end of the war, I did not know. That is what the greatest problem is. And all of a sudden these units appear in that area that are being replaced after given points in time and the commander says, "Who are these people and who are they answerable to?" I cannot give him an answer. Once it's units from Subotica. The next time they're from Ljeskovac. And that is the core of the problem, the lack of re-subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at that point in time, you did not know who ought to command the PJP. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position was that, in accordance with the order of the commander of the army and the Supreme Command Staff, these units should be re-subordinated in the zones of brigades to the commanders of the brigades. That is what was supposed to be the case. However, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what answer did you give the brigade commander? Or did you fail to give him an answer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that point of view, teams from the corps command went to attend mutual meetings of coordination, accommodation of use, if there was no re-subordination because the police did not have an order of their own, then relations of correlation were supposed to be created in order for them to be able to survive the war, everyone within his own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Your Honour, Mr. President, I -- I owe you an answer to a question that was raised yesterday. Those initials from the document P2809. I could not remember the initials NP, whose they were. So with your permission, I was not able to answer. I could not remember yesterday. So may I say that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Colonel Novak Paprica. He is the author of that document dated the 25th of April, P2809. Novak Paprica, a colonel who was in the corps command for a few months. He was there temporarily and he was in the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just need instructions on this. I just have a few questions in relation to some of the topics raised by Mr. Ackerman and that were not present during the examination-in-chief of General Lazarevic. Should I deal with those questions now or after Mr. Hannis' cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's your view on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, yesterday after Mr. Ackerman had asked some questions, during the break I inquired of Mr. Visnjic if that raised something for him. So I was aware that he was going to ask. I have no objection. And I would prefer that he go before me, if you're inclined to permit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to express a concern. There is a procedure that we have set up here that we operate in turn. Mr. Visnjic announced that he had no questions. If I could get to the end of the cross in every case by just saying "no questions," I'd love to go behind Mr. Ivetic, rather than in front of him. So it would seem to me that it would be appropriate that Mr. Visnjic may be allowed to ask questions if he can make a showing that I -- that I raised something that he had no idea that I might raise. I provided a number -- a list of a number of documents that I was going to use. Those documents clearly raised issues. If he has questions relating to those documents, I think it's improper at this point. If it's something outside of the documents - and I don't recall asking very many questions outside of the documents - if it is, then -- then I think, in your discretion, it might be appropriate. But simply to say "no questions" to -- to gain some kind of advantage going behind people who are normally behind you, I think is against the rules we've set up here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While appreciating the mutual convenience that the arrangement proposed might create for Messrs. Visnjic and Hannis, it does seem to us that additional cross-examination should be the exception, rather than the rule, as has been pointed out by Mr. Ackerman and has indeed been the practice that we followed. And the only way we can adjudicate properly on whether Mr. Visnjic should be a second bite at the cherry is when we've heard all the cross-examination and can assess his position in the light of all of the cross-examination. So we require you to proceed at this stage, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I would like to make one comment about that. The reason that I took the position they did was because -- I thought because this was an accused who was testifying. There's -- I see a difference there than with any other witness, because this is not somebody that anybody else could try and recall later on or -- or bring as a rebuttal witness, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that doing it in a slightly different order from the one you propose is going to materially affect that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, and I -- I took Mr. Ackerman's point that there should be a showing made about what was it that you could reasonably anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's also a question of when that showing can best be made, and I think it's later. So let's proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is one procedural matter I wanted to raise with Your Honour. It concerns Exhibit P950, which is the OTP interview of Mr. Lazarevic. It is at e-court, but numbering on the document in e-court is -- is very unhelpful to the reader, because what apparently was done, there were, I don't know, six or seven videotapes of the interview. Each one was translated separately. So the first document you see will say "page 1 of 37." And then the next one is "page 1 of 49." And then "page 1 of 17," et cetera. What I've done is we've made a new copy which has in the lower right-hand corner the number "1" to "264", so the pages are sequential. That matches up with their e-court numbering, 1 through 264. I provided hard copies to each of the Defence counsel on Monday. I have hard copies for each of you Judges and for the Registry and the legal officer. And I would like to make an oral application to substitute this into e-court at the convenient time so that we have a page numbered 1 through 264 version in e-court, which will make it easier for us to follow when I actually get to that document, which won't be today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? No. Very well. We will allow you to substitute this as soon as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And related to that, Judge, we have CDs of -- of the videotapes which we would like to have attached to that in -- in e-court at the -- at the convenient time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have they not already been --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those, I don't believe, were in. It was only the hard copy -- it was only the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you say CDs or DVDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They're on DVDs, but they're computer files, is what my case manager tells me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that means you can see the interview, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not just hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that raises a different issue. Is there any objection to that? Very well. We shall allow you to attach these.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- or good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were commander of the Pristina Corps and particularly during the -- during the war, was a war diary kept at the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of the war, a war diary was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the person or the persons responsible for keeping that war diary?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war diary is kept in the operations organ of the Pristina Corps. It is kept by persons who are on duty service, operations duty officers round the clock, 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you some of the names. Ratko Tesovic, Aleksandar Simonovski, Jovic. I cannot recall his first name now. And a large number of other officers who were on duty at the operations centre of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the investigation of this case and our preparations for trial, the OTP attempted to obtain from the government of Serbia a copy of that war diary. I don't recall the exact wording of the response is, but the essence was that it doesn't exist; it's not in the army archives. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, because my Defence also tried to obtain from the central archives of the Army of Yugoslavia that same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive any explanation or your Defence team receive an explanation about why it's not in the archives? It should be; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it should be. I do not remember that there is an explanation in written form why there is no war diary at the central archives of the Army of Yugoslavia. If you ask me for anything else on that, my own position, my own views, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... they also kept a war diary, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis -- sorry, just a moment, General. I missed who that question related to, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I -- I don't think my entire question was there. I was asking about the forward command post of the Pristina Corps and whether or not they also kept a war diary during the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, the forward command post of the corps did not keep a war diary, as far as I know. Rather, they compiled regular daily combat reports. Some were just written in hand. Others were typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you agree with me it would be helpful to have that document for this court; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. If I'm permitted to say so, the complete reconstruction of what happened in the war, and far more -- and a far more complex one at that, can be based on combat reports of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if in the war diary of the Pristina Corps command information would be kept about your whereabouts on particular days when you were away from the corps command post? Is that the kind of entry that would be put in there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I personally did not have any insight in the keeping of this auxiliary document that is handwritten. I can answer your question with a "yes." It is possible. But I really do not know whether such entries were made. In certain combat reports, that was the case, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of the explanation you got about why it was missing in the archives, was there any information about when it was first discovered that it was not in the archives? Did it actually ever arrive there and then disappear later?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was suggested to my Defence were two ways of seeking this document. One, vis-a-vis the operations administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, because part of the documents from the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps went through the General Staff on their way to the central archives. The second suggestion was to ask the central archives to look through all their documentation in a more detailed fashion. As far as I know, this was dealt with in both ways in great detail, but this war diary was not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But do you know whether or not there was any record indicating that the war diary had actually been received in the archives at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have any insight into the archives list of the central archives, but I believe they would have informed the Defence under what number and when it had arrived. Therefore - and it's just my assumption now - I believe that document did not arrive in the central archives. However, I don't have anything to support this view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe we have a war diary for the forward command post of the 3rd Army. Why wouldn't the Pristina Corps forward command post also keep a war diary?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not just a technical question. At the forward command post of the 3rd Army, there was the army commander personally. At the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, the corps commander was not present. Rather, it was the chief of staff with a group of officers. Therefore, decisions on the use of units took place at the command post of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did no one ever get in -- contact you -- did no one ever from the VJ archives ever get in contact with you about the fact that the war diary was missing and -- to enquire whether you might be able to assist them in locating it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean by that that somebody asked me personally, my answer is "no." But I do have information that the General Staff and the central archives, through the command of the ground forces, which is continuing its obligations and is the tactical -- is tactically responsible for that archives, handed over that archives when the 3rd Army was disbanded and that they were consulted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The interpreter notes that the Pristina Corps was mentioned but she did not catch in what context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that war diary?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't even have this little notebook or notepad like this. I didn't keep even that, let alone the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that my -- the first part of my question was not picked up in the transcript, but I assume that will be listening to the tape. The question was whether or not the general had kept a personal copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll move on. General, I -- before I forget, this is something that came up late yesterday, and I wanted to ask you before I -- I got off into my organised presentation. And it came out that regarding the issue of MUP subordination, that sometime in late April -- and it wasn't clear to me whether it was the 20th or the 22nd -- there was a meeting which you attended with General Pavkovic and, I think, General Stevanovic from the MUP was there. Do you recall that discussion yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that I recalled that we had had a meeting either on the 18th or the 19th. I'm inclined to think it was the 19th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us to the best of your recollection who all attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the army commander ordered that I go with him. I don't know whether General Djakovic was there at the time. I really don't know. I am trying to recall as best I can. And in the course of the night, in a building in Pristina, I remember that General Obrad Stevanovic was there from the police, one of the assistant ministers, and I think General Djordjevic was also there. He was also an assistant to the Minister of the Police for Public Security. I knew what their posts were -- if I knew what they posts were properly then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So on the army side, we have you, General Pavkovic, and perhaps General or -- was he a general at the time, Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was already a general at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So but just three of you from the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about the two of us, the army commander and myself. And I'm just guessing about General Djakovic a bit in a desire to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the army side, only two: General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic. No one else that you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's probably clear, but in the transcript - and I think my learned friend made a slip in his question - "on the army side," General Djordjevic and Stevanovic. They were not on the army side. Probably my learned friend meant to say "on the MUP side."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That -- that's correct. I meant the police side or the MUP side when speaking of General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what building was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- there was no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I saw he said, "I can't recall."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer was, "I can't recall." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall in what building this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. I'm not very familiar with Pristina. It was night-time. The airstrikes were on. So I really can't say. I know we were somewhere upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it must have been fairly close to your command post; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't close. The distance from Pristina to the command post of the corps at the time was about 15 kilometres. To move around under such conditions, when there is a security risk -- no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who arranged the meeting in the first place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for who organised the meeting, I don't know. All I know is that the army commander told me, ordered me, in fact -- he said, "Let's go to see what we'll do about re-subordination," because he had with him a document issued by the Supreme Command on the 18th and he had not yet issued his own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How long did this meeting last approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really hard for me to say, but maybe up to an hour. But I'm really guessing now. We met. We talked. We discussed the topics. Well, up to an hour more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone take notes in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not. I didn't observe the army commander taking notes. As for those two, the two representatives of the MUP, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If General Djakovic had been there, he's most likely the one to have taken notes; correct? He was the note-taker for Joint Command meetings in 1998; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't see him taking notes at those meetings, but I agree with you that if he was there, as the operations man, then he would be the one taking notes. But I'm only guessing when I say that he was with us. It's just guesswork, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there reports generated on your side, on the VJ side after this meeting, either reports up to the Supreme Command Staff about what had taken place or down to subordinate units for information purposes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't do anything either towards my superiors, because he was right next to me, or in relation to my subordinates, because no order had been issued yet. But to the best of my recollection, in the morning - it must have been the 20th - the army commander telephoned the Supreme Command Staff. I didn't follow the conversation, but I know he told me that he had called them up and informed them that the MUP had -- or rather, that the police units in Kosovo and Metohija had not received a document from the Minister of the Interior. That's what the army commander said to me. He told me he had spoken to the Supreme Command Staff. I don't know whether he had spoken to the chief or someone else. And that's how I know this, because he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This -- this issue of MUP subordination or lack of subordination is -- is something that was discussed with you at some length on Friday last week at page 18038.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to wait for Mr. Hannis to round off this topic that he has started and to draw the Court's attention to an assertion made in a question that General Djakovic was the one taking notes. If that relates to that contentious document, there are at least two different handwritings there. And I don't know on what basis the Prosecution can say that General Djakovic attended those meetings at all, let alone that he was the one who took notes. So this is simply leading the witness. There is no evidence on the record so far to support this. I have evidence to the contrary. But the next time I'll rise to my feet a little sooner if this happens once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, questions are not evidence. It's the answers that are evidence. But counsel is entitled to put questions on --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you told us when I'm asking a question that I have to have a basis. I had to read the indictment, and so on. If that is so, I want to know what the basis is for the Prosecutor's question. Otherwise, it's a capricious question, as we call it in our system.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And such questions in my system are not permitted. That's two questions in one. What if he had said "yes"? To what part of the question would his answer have related?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you quite -- are you quite finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I was going to say to you that albeit there may not be evidence on the record in relation to this, if a party has information on which it is appropriate to found a question, then the question becomes appropriate because the issue may arise later or that the evidence may come in later. And it's only right that all the issues should have been explored at the appropriate time. Now, my recollection so far - and perhaps it's wrong and we'll have it corrected - is that we've been told already how these documents came into the possession of the Prosecution as a foundation for the questions. And my recollection is that Djakovic was mentioned as involved in the exercise of producing these on the basis of information available to the Prosecution. Now, is that wrong, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall specifically what's in the record concerning that. I know there may have been something in a 65 ter, because he was a potential witness. But I can assure the Court and Mr. Fila I have a good-faith basis for asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes. And indeed, the 65 ter in relation to Djakovic and Mr. Ackerman's list would be enough foundation for these questions to be asked. So we are very clear on the difference between questions and answers, Mr. Fila. The fact that the questions asked does not establish for one minute that Djakovic wrote these minutes. On the other hand, the witness has added to our information because of the question that was put by telling us that he would be the obvious man, if he was at the meeting, to make notes, whatever you call them. So we shall repel the objection and continue with the evidence. Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A matter which is concerning Judge Chowhan, Mr. Hannis, is that at line 24 on page 32 - really line 25 - you pose two questions. And the answer is therefore open to misunderstanding. To which meetings was the witness referring in that answer. So you should try to clarify that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I guess I did ask you two questions and you gave one answer, and I don't know if the answer was for the first question, the second question, or both. Are you aware from your attendance at some meetings called Joint Command meetings in August and September of 1998 who kept notes of those meetings? That was General Djakovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that I didn't know -- that I didn't see anyone taking notes at those meetings, including Djakovic. I didn't see that. I didn't see anyone taking notes at that meeting. That was my answer. You then asked me about another meeting between the army commander, myself, and two members of the MUP on the 19th of April in connection with re-subordination, and you said, "Had Djakovic been there, would he have been the one taking notes?" I said I didn't take notes, the army commander didn't, but he might have done as the operations man. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you two questions to supplement that. Do you recollect whether Djakovic was at any of the Joint Command meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I was there, except for a few people, I can't remember -- there were 10 or 12 of these. I know I was with the army commander. And I really cannot identify the people from the police or the state security. And I said that last time. Because I happened to be there ad hoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was Djakovic there, who's neither from the police or the state --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall, Your Honour, that Djakovic was there at the time I was there. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- the second question I have is: Assuming he was for the moment there, would your position be the same, that if anyone were to make notes, it would be him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a bit different. Let me say that those were informal meetings. We had coffee. We exchanged information. And at such meetings, at least to the best of my knowledge, there was no one taking notes. Because these were not official meetings. This serious task that the army commander and I set out to perform to talk about a task issued by the Supreme Command concerning re-subordination. Had someone else been there, I allowed for the possibility. But neither the army commander nor I took notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note your answer. Mr. Hannis, are you going to be exploring the nature of the meetings which the witness has described as "informal meetings" and which have been described as "Joint Command meetings" in the course of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Indeed I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may -- I may go to some of that immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. There's no need for us to take that any further at this stage. We'll break now and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I wanted to advise the Court that I will get into evidence about Joint Command meetings and this -- this accused's attendance at those meetings, but I want to do it a little later. And with regard to the basis for my question, I want to indicate I checked the 65 ters. The original 65 ter file with regard to the Witness Djakovic on the 15th of June, 2007 only says he will describe his attendance at Joint Command meetings in 1998. He will provide his impression on certain documents with regarding the Joint Command in 1998. My basis for asking about, offering the notes or the minutes is based on an unsigned statement by him from an interview conducted by Mr. Coo and Ms. Grogan which was disclosed to the Defence in connection with his anticipated testifying here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I wanted to ask you about your -- your answers to some questions that were put to you last Friday by your counsel and then by Judge Bonomy concerning this issue of subordination of the MUP. And in that discussion, Judge Bonomy, at page 18038 asked you: "Mr. Lazarevic, who was your opposite member in the MUP in Kosovo?" And in your answer, you said: "I would like to know that after all these years. I stand here in front of you as an accused and yet I don't know that." So you even now don't know who your counterpart in the MUP was in Kosovo in 1998? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is that this is not a question of counterparts. The military and the police are institutions that are far too different. As far as I can remember my entire answer now, I also added that I'm not the one who is supposed to seek a counterpart or subordinates. I should, rather, get from my superior information on who is being re-subordinated to me. I did not get that from the army commander because he did not get that from the Supreme Command Staff in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you not make any efforts at that time to try and figure out who you could or should speak to about this issue of subordination? Didn't you at least take that minimal step?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of these minimal steps was made on the 19th by the army commander. And I was present there and this was with two assistant ministers of the interior. That was the initial step. After that, I sent my own teams at the level of the Secretariat of the Interior and at the level of police detachments in the field to see whether there could be some kind of cooperation if re-subordination was impossible. I assure you once again that I cannot with assistant Ministers of the Interior discuss that, debate these matters. I receive my orders from the army commander as to what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- When this topic came up and when there was some extended discussion about it, why didn't you mention then this meeting that you and Pavkovic had with Djordjevic and Stevanovic? Don't you think that was pertinent to the issue?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to that meeting of the 19th, I did participate together with the army commander. We certainly did talk up to one hour how and what, and I explained how that meeting ended. The two MUP representatives explained that they could not carry out orders of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff because they did not have an order from their own minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear about what exactly you're saying here. Am I right in recollecting that once you were instructed, sometime after the 20th of April, to try effectively to re-subordinate the MUP, I think you described that as "mission impossible."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, what you've referred to now is what I wanted to say; namely, that the army commander, in addition to his first order of the 20th of April, issued yet another order or two in which he asks me, after all these deadlines, to carry out this task. Since that could not have been done even at that stage, he simply stopped dealing with that and stopped asking me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you described it as "mission impossible"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I described it as "mission impossible" and I explained why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you've told us both in answer to, I think, Mr. Ivetic and in answer to Mr. Hannis about this meeting, so there was an effort at the level of Pavkovic, certainly, to address the issue, how you do it. And then after that meeting, you've just told us you dispatched --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's no interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there now interpretation? All right. So you told us today and, I think, now on two occasions about a meeting where you accompanied General Pavkovic. And that meeting was to address the difficulty of re-subordination. And you've told us that following the meeting you told your various subordinates to liaise with the equivalent MUP personnel to try to achieve that. Now, why is it you're exempt in the middle of all this from -- from having an obligation to meet somebody at your level to try to make it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I did not say to subordinate units to find their own counterparts, equivalents. But from a nonexisting order of the superior command, I wrote my own order, to the extent to which I knew where what MUP units were at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To have brigade commanders find those MUP units on the ground and try to establish contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's not bandy words on this. Your words were in English: "After that" -- that's after the meeting -- "I sent my own teams at the level of the Secretariat of the Interior and at the level of police detachments in the field to see whether there could be some kind of cooperation if re-subordination was impossible." Now, that suggests to me that you were telling those beneath you to try to liaise with the police to make the order that you had been given work in some way. And we've heard about the meeting that you attended in the company of General Pavkovic. And my simple question is: Why is it you in the middle of all this didn't have to look for a counterpart to try to discuss making it work? What's so different about your level of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, what you are saying now is the second step that I took as commander after the order sending a command group out into the field. Now I'm returning to your concrete question. In Pristina, in Kosovo and Metohija, there was a MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. And I was not aware of their composition. Two assistant ministers came to that staff or were on that staff, two assistant Ministers of the Interior. The commander of the army talked to them; I talked to them. In the order of the army commander, it says: "Units and organs of the MUP." That is to say, of public security and state security should be re-subordinated. Which ones? That is not written anywhere. How? That is not written either. Who should do this? That's not written either. I tried to explain to you what it was that I tried, as commander at this operative level, to do so that out in the field where people are losing lives, where the defence of the country is taking place, to prevent graver consequences from ensuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have to go back, because I don't think you answered my question at page 40, line 13. I asked you: Why, when this topic came up on Friday, and your counsel and Judge Bonomy were asking you about it, and I think Judge Bonomy asked you a question along the lines about your telling us that you were persistent in trying to do something about it; what steps did you take? Why didn't you not mention last Friday this meeting with the assistant minister, Djordjevic, and General Stevanovic? Isn't that probably the most significant meeting you had with the police about subordination? Why didn't you mention it then?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was answering my attorney's questions as to what it was that I did after the 20th of April when I issued the order on re-subordination. I was explaining that part. Secondly, this meeting was a meeting that the army commander ordered me to have, and for me he is the mainstay of that meeting. He ordered me to follow that. I did not do that on my own bat. I talked about my own activities and my own measures. When Defence counsel, Mr. Ivetic, asked me about this, then I gave a concrete answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Judge Bonomy, at page 18039, line 13 said: "Now, it sounds as though you didn't make any effort to liaise with someone at your level in the MUP to try to achieve that." And in your answer just now, you said, I guess, one of your reasons for not mentioning this meeting with Djordjevic and Stevanovic is because this meeting was a meeting that the army commander ordered me to have. He ordered me to follow that. I did not do that on my own bat. I talked about my own activities and my own measures." So are you telling us because General Pavkovic ordered you to go to the meeting, you didn't think you needed to mention it when this issue about efforts to liaise with the MUP about subordination was being discussed? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that as for the assistant ministers of the interior, I cannot discuss a task with them that was ordered by the President of the State. For the umpteenth time, I'm trying to say that with the army commander I did participate in such a meeting. And thirdly, that after the 20th, within my own scope of work, I did things - I hope that you will be assured of this through documents and through the witnesses who are yet to come - I took many measures at tactical level to have this done; namely, what I called "mission impossible."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you knew who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I just was trying to clarify a point. Now, obviously you were going to the field. You were working there in a geographical area. The question is: How would you work in a vacuum? Because anybody who is pitted with such a -- such a task, such a situation as you were would know the other factors with whom he would be dealing and knowing about your counterpart or less than a counterpart in the MUP was something very obvious. This information, you required, you needed for -- for interacting with the -- with those people present there. And it is very strange that we are unable to get an answer from you with respect to the name of that person. Now, that is something which I'm really surprised at. I wonder if you can -- you can answer that. Because any commander, any centurion, whatever, working in the field has to know the whereabouts, the names of persons around that place where he is working, even if he is not a part of those people. I'm sorry, General, to burden you with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right when you ask me this way. At that time, I would have wanted to know who they were and where they were. Yet again I kindly ask the Honourable Trial Chamber to understand this sentence that: "Organs and units of the MUP shall be re-subordinated." Even today from this place where I am here and now, I don't know what this means. The centres of state security are there. All institutions are there. That is not the way military orders are issued. You are now asking me to say who it was that I was looking for. In the field through brigade commanders, who are out there in the field, who know chiefs of the SUP, of the Ministry of the Interior, at this tactical level I asked them to find people and to establish contact with them. And I sent my own assistant commanders to help in this correlation at this tactical level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, by this time, in -- in late April, mid-or late April, your subordinate units had already carried out dozens or scores of actions against -- against the terrorist, or the KLA. And are you telling us in spite of all those joint actions with the MUP, you didn't know who was in charge of the MUP in Kosovo? You were there in Pristina. They were just across the street, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect to Their Honours, I was not across the street from any MUP structure. I might have been on the first day, but after that neither did they know where I was nor did I know where they were. That's one thing. And the second thing is, I know for a fact in the initial period of the war that these anti-rebel actions supports to the MUP units took place in precisely defined chains of command, as we say. The units of the Pristina Corps were commanded by the brigade commands and the corps command and the MUP units had their intact chain of command within the framework of coordination. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not trying to tell us that you wouldn't have been able to find them if you wanted to, are you? I mean the MUP commanders or superiors in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir, that I said I asked for particular members of the MUP or that they asked for me. What I understood you to be asking me about was the initial period of the war, from the -- around the 20th of April or thereabouts, when anti-rebel actions were conducted without the formal order which arrived on re-subordination. That was the context of my reply when I said that the units had the task of coordinating these activities on the ground. By Their Honours' leave, we have an exhibit here dated the 9th of April where I ordered that the commanders get in touch with five Secretariats of the Interior, which were planning certain actions in order to coordinate certain activities, to see what could be done, to report back to me so that I as the commander could verify the possibility of participating in these actions. That was the gist of my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, during that time, you knew who General Sreten Lukic was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who General Sreten Lukic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you try to get in touch with him about this issue of subordination to find out if he was your counterpart or, if not, whether he could tell you who that would be that you should speak to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not try to solve that problem with General Lukic, because, I repeat, two members of the police of higher rank than he was told the army commander and myself that they could not implement that task. On the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what do you recall about what they said about why they could not implement the task? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was discussion, to the best of my recollection, of the practical possibilities or impossibilities of re-subordination of MUP units to the army in a true combat sense, as provided for in the rules of combat of the army, and not as the legislator in the Law on Defence said in a single sentence, which can be interpreted in every which way. We discussed what units might possibly be included in the execution of combat tasks and which could not. Furthermore, they had a system of regular changes of manpower. In the army, when you're holding positions, that is simply impossible. And finally, what I recall very well from all that was said was the conclusion reached by one of those two Assistant Ministers of the Interior, who said, "We cannot implement this because we do not have an order from our minister."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of that, you left the meeting with the impression that this was, to use your earlier term, this was "mission impossible"; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- well, first of all, did you yourself report this up to the Supreme Command Staff, this meeting and the results of the meeting, MUP's position?
