utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I beg you to understand that I have neither the right nor the duty to report to the Supreme Command Staff on the realization of tasks ordered by the Supreme Command Staff. That is something done by the army command. In the course of today, I testified that the army commander told me that on the following day, the 20th, he rang up the Supreme Command Staff and informed them, and that was his duty. It was up to him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Pavkovic reported up to the Supreme Command Staff about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it has been answered, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so you took no further steps to liaise at your level because you thought this was impossible and you had more important things to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, these questions are being asked over and over and over. This is about the fourth time that question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he's answered it about four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions there, Mr. Hannis, and I wonder if either of them is going to add anything to our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll move on. [Microphone not activated] You mentioned in the beginning of your testimony about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in the beginning of your testimony how you came to be at the Pristina Corps. And you were shown an order signed by General Perisic concerning that transfer. You told us, however, that you had never seen it until a few months ago and that at the time you had acted on oral orders. And that was one way that business was conducted in the army, that you used oral orders as well as written orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oral orders by the commander is a legitimate method of issuing combat tasks, orders, and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you used that as a commander yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain circumstances, on certain occasions, especially when there was no telecommunications system in place which could deal with written orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also told us about your commendation. When were you commended?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak about my commendation. What I did say was that I was not commended in May 1999, in early May, as one witness claimed. And this can be seen in column 15 of my personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, when were you commended? I don't have your personnel file in front of me. Can you please tell us when you were commended.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my file, as far as I can recall - because I don't have it before me either now - I think I was not commended but awarded a prize, an official pistol, after the war by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2000, to the best of my recollection now. And that has been entered into my personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that General Pavkovic who was the Chief of Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the best of my recollection, the Chief of the General Staff at that time was General Ojdanic. I was the corps commander. General Pavkovic was the army commander. So in 1999 and 2000, that's possible. Certainly after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I noticed in the early parts of your testimony and on several occasions you -- you talked about what was happening in Kosovo in 1998. You referred to "the armed rebellion." I think at page 17749, you said: "In June the armed rebellion in Kosovo spread to Djakovica and Decani municipalities." That's correct in your view, isn't it, that by this stage what was happening was an armed rebellion more than mere terrorism? Right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military knowledge, which I admit is modest when it comes to this topic, is that a forcible attempt to topple the constitutional order is called "an armed rebellion." And this attempt to topple the constitutional order by force is something I refer to as an officer as "an armed rebellion." And in the documents of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, in General Perisic's time, and in the directive this term is used, "armed rebellion."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the -- the state authorities had reluctance to use that term to describe what was happening in Kosovo because of possible implications it might carry with regard to international law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the state authorities were doing in regard to defining the security problems for the state on Kosovo and Metohija. I didn't see any of these documents or hear any of those statesmen speaking. I didn't see any of them. But from what I myself experienced on the border with Albania for more than a year, what I saw and experienced for myself led me to have no doubt that this was a classical terrorist armed rebellion according to any category of military science in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were aware, however, that in July of 1998 that the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, expressed concern about how the army was being used and suggested his desire that a state of emergency should be declared so the army could engage against these terrorists in areas outside the border belt. You knew about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are talking about is something I know about from documents I have seen in these proceedings. At that time, in 1998 and throughout 1999, up until recently, I really did not have any information about what General Perisic asked from whom. I had occasion to meet him more than once in Kosovo and Metohija, but I really have no contemporaneous knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This wasn't a matter that was discussed in your presence? You never heard General Pavkovic mention this during 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 17749 you told us that you had intelligence about the terrorists or the KLA arming children aged 16. How do you know about that? Do you have documents to show that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was a Prosecution document we commented on. It wasn't intelligence information. It was a Prosecution document about a meeting in the Dukagjini area. I am really trying not to interrupt my learned friend, but I would kindly ask him to make an effort to present the exhibits correctly, as they were presented here, so as not to mislead the witness. I'm sure that's not his intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, we take the view that Mr. Hannis is perfectly entitled to ask the question he asked the way he did. This is cross-examination and he's entitled to test the personal knowledge of the witness. You've largely presented his evidence through a series of -- of leading questions, which is understandable, because you were basing your case very largely on the documents that he was personally familiar with. And that was not inappropriate. However, there can be more value in testing personal -- direct personal knowledge, and Mr. Hannis did not in that question present anything misleading, albeit the Prosecution may have documents. The likely source of these documents is the Army of Yugoslavia. So we would prefer that you did not interrupt to discuss the detail of the potential answer unless there's something plainly unfair about the question that's been asked, and this was not a question that falls into that category. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me rephrase that question. At page 17749, line 14, you said, General: "They mobilised children age 16. And if the Trial Chamber allows me to explain why I know that, I know that because those villages were, for the most part, Catholic villages and they applied to the military and to the Minister of Interior. They wanted us to protect them. They didn't want to take up those weapons and they didn't want to side with the armed rebellion." Now, there was a document that Mr. Bakrac showed you from -- from KLA purportedly, but my question is: Did you have some documents at that time that reflected this? In 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. The corps command - I am primarily referring to the forward command post - and I'm talking about my personal knowledge. Well, we had operative information about the arming of minors. We talked to people from these villages. They said to the military security organs that even children were given weapons and we also captured a group of terrorists that was trying to cross the border that included minors who were in uniform and armed. I really ask that we be very accurate. This document that we used is not from the army. It is from the so-called General Staff of the KLA. And we offered that as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I agree, we should try to be accurate. I did say that was a document purportedly from the KLA. You said just now that you're talking about your personal knowledge: "We talked to people from these villages." Did you talk to people from these Catholic villages personally?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one occasion very well. As chief of staff of the corps - and I think that the corps commander was there too - we visited a village in the border area towards Kosare. I think it's called Batusa. We talked to the local population there that the soldiers were passing that way in order to guard the border and to guard them. We were telling them not to take weapons from anyone. We brought them quite a bit of food supplies. And they accepted what it was that we were saying, these proposals, and they promised that they would do their best not to take terrorist forces in. In the village of Batusa this was done to a considerable degree; however, later on many soldiers got killed in that area. So, yes, on one occasion quite certainly - I remember that - and it's the village of Batusa. That is, June 1998. That is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of June 1998. There is a video recording of that. There is evidence of that. But I am referring to that by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in the answer you've just given, you've not given any indication of what, if anything, you may have learned on that occasion about the particular issue that Mr. Hannis is asking you. Please try to listen to what the question is about and -- and deal with the question. I don't know if Mr. Hannis wishes to pursue it to find out if there is an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to follow up on another part of the earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also said before, General, that -- that you captured a group coming across the border that included minors. When was that? Is that reflected in any report that you have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April onwards, there were quite a few times that this happened. This is contained in the combat reports of the 3rd Army. And I remember that what followed was an order of the corps commander that additional measures should be taken with a view to preventing incursions by terrorist forces from Albania because they are putting children into their first lines and we do not want these minors to get hurt in clashes with border security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's your definition of minor? Under what age?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that I mean what the Law on the Army says. That is, military age, when people are eligible to do their military service. And that is the age of 18 onwards. So when I say "minor," I mean under the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You said -- you talked about these villagers from the Catholic villages. What part of Kosovo are we talking about? Are we talking about on the -- on the west side of Kosovo? Between Djakovica and Pec?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: South-west, geographically speaking. And I'm specifically referring to the villages around Djakovica. I am referring to the village of Korenica, Doblibare, and a few others, in the broader area of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about Guska? That was a small village near Korenica, as I recall. That was a Catholic village. No?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Guska is one that I know. And as far as I can remember, it is in that area, but I cannot be very specific on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if these villagers were asking you and the MUP to protect them, why in April 1999 were the VJ and the MUP cleaning out those villages, specifically Korenica and Guska, as we heard from Merita Deda and Lizane Malaj earlier in this case? You recall their testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the testimony of Merita Deda and some others. You're asking me why the army and the police cleansed those villages. I can say to you what it is that I know; namely, that in that area at that time there were several hundred terrorists, members of the armed rebellion. There was an entire brigade that clashed with the security forces. Further on, what happened specifically is what we heard of from these witnesses. I'm not aware of the details, but people who took part in all of that will be coming here, and I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take note of that and to allow these witnesses, the participants in these events, to speak about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, and during the cleansing of those villages and the clash with the terrorists, the civilians were told to go to Albania; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about any one of the members of the corps units having ordered any civilian from that area or from any other Albania to go to -- any other area to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any information about members of the MUP telling those civilians to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information about any of the members of the MUP doing that. I have no such information. And in particular - and I say "in particular" - I am saying that I don't have such reports from army unit, because it's army units that I got my reports from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you have any information about civil protection, civil defence, or the armed non-Siptar population telling those civilians from the villages or Korenica and Guska to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I am talking about information from units that were in that area. It is only natural that my answer does not pertain to what it was that we heard here from Prosecution witnesses. Once again, I repeat that I did not have any information about any structures of the state organs in the defence system expelled the civilian population from that area or from some other area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall protected Witness K73 who testified here about events in that area in late April 1999? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few -- or rather, quite a few witnesses with that pseudonym, "K." If you could please be so kind as to ... Well, not give me the name, but I don't know how you can help me answer your question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You may remember him because before he left the courtroom, as I recall, I think he clicked his heels together and gave you a head nod before he left the room. Do you remember that? Now you know who I'm talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, now I know who it is that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So do you recall his testimony about what he was doing with his unit and what he saw in that area regarding the moving-out of the population?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall in principle what his testimony was during those days, on the 27th and 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that he was not truthful or accurate about what he described in his experience during that operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the witness statement of K73 from the level of his duty about an action that is called an "operation" here, can be at this lowest level. The insight that he can have into everything that was happening -- well, I can assess it, but I cannot deal with it. I'm trying to say that that is his view or that is his statement. I want to say to the Trial Chamber that I hope a witness from that period of time will come, an officer, who took part in that assignment and who was the superior of that person, so then we can find out a bit more about whether he was telling the truth or whether he was not telling the truth and whether he had enough information or whether he did not have enough information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, K73 talked about seeing the civilians and being received as sort of -- at the end of the road they were coming down, as K73 and those on -- those neighbours to his units on either side were driving people in that direction. Do you recall he talked about the men were separated out and the women and children were directed on down the road? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not recall that statement that K73 stated that. Would it be possible for the transcript to be shown to me? But I really do not recall that he said that his unit at the rank of a platoon or two took part in the separation from men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we have time, General, maybe we'll do that later. Let me move on to another topic at the moment. You mentioned a couple of classical terrorist tactics. One of them you called the." "1.000 fires tactic." The second one you mentioned was the -- the two -- "The two villages tactic." At page 17754 you described this is one where one villages is evacuated of civilians, and it then constitutes a fortified military territory stronghold; whereas, in the second village is concentrated the civilian population, which extends logistical and other support, is also a live shield. I'm not clear on how this works. It sounds like what you're describing is one village is -- is fortified and that's what's used by the terrorist and the civilians are in the second village. So why don't you just attack the fortified village? I understand you say that they may use it as a shield, but can't you go around to the other side? Or am I being too simple-minded about all that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to use a specific authentic factual example to explain this terrorist tactic. The village of Smonica, which has been mentioned in this courtroom more than once, was a purely paramilitary terrorist stronghold at a high level. On the main road between Djakovica and Decani and several border posts. The entire area in front of the village was fortified and mines were laid there and there were no, or very few, civilians there. The civilians from that village had been moved to the village of Nec, the village of Nivokaz, the village of Birjak [phoen], and the village of Smonica as a terrorist stronghold could not be approached without passing through the villages to which the civilians had been evacuated. So what you are saying -- or rather, your question was why the terrorist stronghold was not attacked. When on the 2nd of August the Chief of Staff of the army ordered that this terrorist stronghold be neutralised, there was a lot of tactics on the part of the units and a lot of restraint needed to carry out this extremely difficult task. The terrorist stronghold was neutralised but they went to these villages and got mixed in with the civilians, and that was the end of the action, because one could not chase and destroy them, since they had become mixed up with the civilians. That was the tactic I mentioned, which I am now trying to explain so everyone will understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, it seems to me that that's a -- a very good explanation for why it was decided -- or why the action was taken later to remove all the civilians, because of this very problem that the terrorist, the KLA, would fight until they decided it was better to slip away. And as you've told us -- we've heard other witnesses indicate sometimes they changed into civilian clothes and mixed in with the civilian population. This was a very frustrating situation for the army and the MUP, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I cannot agree with this statement concerning frustration or lack of it, especially as regards what was done. I mentioned the date in August 1998. I assume you are referring to the wartime period six or eight months later, and these two -- these things have nothing to do with each other, and especially not with some sort of systematic large-scale campaign of attacking Albanian villages or a widespread attack to eliminate all that from the area by the army and the MUP, as you say. So my answer is no, that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect back to you, General, I would say that not everyone in your army would agree or not everyone in the MUP would agree that this was not frustrating, trying to fight this kind of enemy who hid, who ambushed, who fired until they saw it was advantageous to leave and then slip into civilian clothes and mix in with the villagers so you couldn't pursue them any further. And this after having killed or wounded one's colleagues in the VJ and the MUP. Are you seriously telling me that the average MUP policeman or the average VJ soldier engaged in those operations would not find that frustrating at least?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ask leave as far as possible to explain that I cannot talk about the MUP from every possible aspect concerning the army. I am neither competent nor authorised nor do I have the required knowledge. But when I said that members of the army were not frustrated with this tactic, members of the army have to respond to enemy tactics with certain tactical actions, whether they be frustrated or not. In the army, one acts precisely according to certain principles, regulations, and orders, not by responding emotionally. If such things happen, they're isolated cases, but that's not what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you're not giving yourself enough credit. I think you are competent and authorised, because I'm not necessarily talking about MUP versus VJ as being different somehow. This is a very human situation. You're a human being. You've been a soldier. You know about combat. How can you sit there and tell me with a straight face that a person engaged in that kind of situation would not find it frustrating? You see your buddy injured or killed. You know it came from over there. You don't know which one of those so-and-sos did it. But eventually aren't you going to reach the point where you want to get even? Isn't that human nature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Hannis wishes to transform the accused into an expert for psychology or psychiatry, for him to tell us whether someone was frustrated or not. I don't think that falls within the scope of his testimony, and that's my objection. I'm doing my best not to interrupt. This is the second time I have risen to my feet. But now I really think that we are asking the accused to be an expert witness, a neuropsychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you must object when you consider it appropriate. Our concern is that these objections should not consist of a narrative of a possible answer for the witness or a discussion of the evidence, where that can be avoided. And therefore it's important, obviously, to confine those which require substantial discussion to situations which necessarily involve some sort of prejudice to the witness. On this question, we shall confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the question that has been asked requires the sort of opinion that anyone familiar with human behaviour and human emotion and reaction can give. So far as that is of any use to the Tribunal in determining the issue, it's not a matter that requires expert evidence, so we will repel the objection which is founded on that basis but observe that one wonders what value there might be in view of the fact that the witness has twice addressed the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honours. I don't want to speak in front of the accused, but quite simply the question always contains a trap. And as the trap is evident, it can be avoided. And then we get ourselves into a situation like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I've made the ruling. See, what you have to be very careful about in this situation is that unlike the position with other witnesses, we cannot ask this witness to be removed from the courtroom while we discuss the rights or wrongs of a question. That's why greater caution is required when an accused is giving evidence. You understand? That's why I am -- I am particularly concerned about this problem. So when we make a ruling, that is the ruling to be followed. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In -- in light of your remarks, I will move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to show you Exhibit P1428. I've actually got a hard copy I can hand you, if the usher can assist. This is a Pristina Corps command decision dated the 14th of August, 1998. You saw this one before. This is one that you signed yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is -- well, this is a good time to ask you this question: Could you explain for me the difference for you between an operation and an action, in terms of activities by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An action is a form of combat action at the lowest tactical level within the framework of tactical and joint tactical units, and the numbers involved are 100 men or fewer to up to several hundred or several thousand men. In this particular action specifically, there was Combat Group 15-3, which contain 197 persons. An operation, on the other hand, is the most complex form of combat action carried out on a large area according to a certain plan and has as its aim an operative or a strategic goal. It has the highest possible goal to be achieved through the carrying-out of the operation. For example, the overall engagement of the Pristina Corps in the defence of the country is called a defensive operation of the Pristina Corps. That was the only one, and it lasted for the three months of the war. Everything else within this single operation that had strategic or operative aims of defending the integrity of the country, there were hundreds of battles, fights, ambushes, incursions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is anything less than the overall engagement of the Pristina Corps in the defence of the country during the 78 days of the war, is anything less than that then something that I should refer to as "an action" instead of "an operation"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. An action, a fight, or a battle, according to the combat rules. There's only one operation, and within that operation there are actions, battles, fights, certain tactical activities, and all those lower level activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, and, General, I'll try to do that but I think it may be a matter of translation. I seem to recall some of the documents referring to specific actions in a smaller geographic area over a couple of days being referred to as "operations." And I note under item 1 here, the last line says: "Readiness for operations at 0700 hours on 15 August."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Readiness for activities on the 15th of August." That's what it says in the Serbian version, in this document signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that was Mr. Hannis' question. And to avoid confusion, in the English version it does say "forces for diversion operations." But I would like the general to read out what it says in the original, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that might be an idea in this case, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if you could read the last line under item number 1. The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Readiness for activities on the 15th of August, 1998 at 0700 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, my English translation -- says "operations." That's one we'll -- we'll check on. General, this -- these activities or this action was to break up sabotage and terrorist forces in the Slup and Voksa villages sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was an action to break up sabotage and terrorist forces in the Slup and Voksa villages sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in this particular action, you were in charge; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th Armoured Brigade was the one conducting these activities, with its Combat Group 15-3. I was at the forward command post in Djakovica at that time. There was a team from the General Staff there with me, some dozen officers, who at that time were inspecting or controlling the corps units. General Perisic was there. Certainly I monitored what was going on. But if you are referring to my signing this document, that doesn't mean that I was in command of that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, who was in command of the action, then? Are you saying it was the -- the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade, or it was General Perisic, or -- or who?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 15th Armoured Brigade. And if you allow my to say this, we showed the order of the brigade commander for that action, this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then let's have a look at the meetings of the Joint Command for 1998. This is Exhibit P1468. I'd like to go to page 54 of the English. And I think it's page -- I believe it's page 45 of the B/C/S, but I've got a -- I've got a hard copy of the page I want to ask you about. And I've -- I've highlighted the portion there where General Pavkovic is speaking. And it appears to be about the fifth or sixth -- the sixth bullet point down. In English, it's translated as saying: "The Chief of Staff would command the action around Vonca [phoen] and Stanpul [phoen]." I suggest to you based on other evidence, including 1428, that that is a misreading of the handwriting in B/C/S and should refer to "Voksa" and "Slup." Correct? Because this is from a meeting on the 13th of August, 1998. That's what General Pavkovic was talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read this in the Serbian language as it's written here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read out --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the part that refers to the villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The action around Voksa and Slup would be under the Chief of Staff." It does not say "shall command." It says "would," in the conditional. That is how somebody wrote this, that it would be led by. "Rukovodi."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a difference in the Serbian language between "command" and "control." And this -- well, I'll try to follow your instructions. I would kindly ask the interpreters to try to make this distinction, because the general read out here "would be." He didn't say "command."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: We said "under." We did not say "command." And the word used is "rukovodio" which is word from the noun, "control." So it would be "under the control of."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way it was translated into English there was "would be led by," which is yet a third way of -- of describing it. I wonder if it matters -- I wonder if it matters for the purpose of the examination. I doubt it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not a lot, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I have a question based on the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's -- let's proceed with this. And if a formal translation -- retranslation is required, then the document can be -- or the page can be re-submitted to CLSS and then filed by whichever party wishes us to take notice of something which has not been made clear in the course of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, could you explain to me what the difference is between an operation being commanded by you and one being under you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in essence, there is a difference if the Chief of Staff is the person who commands. Then he issues assignments to all the engaged forces, makes decisions, amends the decision, receives reports, and monitors the implementation of that decision. If somebody else is the mainstay, then this other person, the commander of the brigade of the -- or the combat group, carries out these tasks. I'm saying this from the point of view of command. However, you asked me, I think - at least, that's the translation I got - you asked me what the difference was between "command" and "control." Control, "rukovodjenje," is a broader notion in terms of directing, organising, and coordinating all these activities. But there is no direct command. Direct command is in somebody else's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in your answer you just said, "There's a difference if the Chief of Staff is the person who commands. Then he issues assignments to all the engaged forces, makes decisions." In P1428, signed by you, this is a document that's called a decision, and it has "task for units." So isn't that what you're doing? Isn't that exactly what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, that is not the way it is. We, my Defence, displayed at least four documents in respect of this action the other day. First of all, the commander of the 3rd Army made the decision for this action. Secondly, that the corps command made a decision. And on the map up -- this was approved to him by the commander of the 3rd Army. Fourthly, that the commander of the 3rd Army -- or rather, the corps commander reported to the army commander about this action. I, as chief of staff, signed this part because on that day the commander was not there. He was accompanying the Chief of General Staff so that the units could be prepared for this task. In order for me to command the units, I have to have authorisation from my commander that I can command the units and use the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Just for the transcript, I wanted to draw your attention to one thing. There is a problem with interpretation because Mr. Hannis keeps using the word "operation." Look at 12, 71. He's asking General Lazarevic what the difference is between these operations, when he -- he commands an operation or somebody lower than him; whereas, what this is about is an action. I don't want this to create problems for you. There is no action -- there is no operation involved here. That is what the word used in the -- this so-called document is "action" as well. So we are only talking about action, not operations here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which line were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 71, line 12. So it's Mr. Hannis' question. It says "operation." And that word is not mentioned anywhere. So it's 12. The question that was put to General Lazarevic: What is the difference between you commanding an operation or a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't find -- I can't find it. Which line is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6/7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 71. 7. I saw it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Hannis accept what accepts what you say in view of the definitions he's already had from the witness of these two expressions. Thank you. We shall rise until five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't know, do you still have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now -- actually, I was specifically referring to P1428, the decision on the 14th of August. Do you have that? I see you have the -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In one of your last answers before the break, you said in order for you to command the units, you would have to have authorisation from your commander. Well, you did have authorisation for this particular action, didn't you? I mean, we see General Pavkovic on the 13th of August is telling the Joint Command meeting that this -- this action in the Slup and Voksa area would be under you; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber, I will repeat that that is not what is written there. What is written there is "would be under the control." So this is the conditional. It does not say "will" or"shall" be under the control of. So what this person who was at the meeting wrote does not mean that an order was issued to me that I command that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, apart from what that person wrote at the meeting, did General Pavkovic tell you that you would be in charge of that action? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then how is it that you're issuing a decision assigning tasks to those various groups? Did you do that without his permission?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations organ of the corps command that planned this task, being unable at that point in time to find the corps commander to sign this decision, brought it to me, the chief of staff, who does have the right to sign such a document. I recalled that the corps command had already signed that decision on the decision map and it had been approved by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you said that the person who wrote what happened at the informal meeting used the conditional tense and the word "would." What was the condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It probably depended on where the corps commander would be at that point in time. As he was touring the units with the Chief of General Staff, it depend on whether he would get to the forward command post in Djakovica or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Pavkovic knew ahead of time that he was going to be touring with General Perisic, and that's why he arranged for you to be in control of this action; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered twice. If the Trial Chamber so requests, I will do it a third time. That is not what is written here, and that is not the order that I received, executive, as orders are in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then did you receive an order about this and what was your order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few moments ago, I explained that I had not received an order, that at that time I was reporting to a big team from the General Staff about securing the state border. The focus of the control inspection was in Djakovica, in that part of the units. I went with that team to the units. This control inspection went on for three days precisely in Djakovica, and that is what General Obradovic testified about as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, we've seen other documents, orders, decisions, reports, et cetera, which may have the typewritten name of the superior commander but it's signed for that person by a subordinate. Why wasn't this signed "za"? Why wasn't this signed for Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Pavkovic? If it says "commander," I'm the only one who can sign it. But if it says "chief of staff" then there's no "za," for, then I sign it. Had this said "commander," "komandant," General Pavkovic, then I could have signed it along with the word "za," for. However, since it was printed out "Chief of Staff" I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I thought from your earlier answer you said the reason that you signed this was because the commander was not available. But why is it compared with your typewritten name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, because the commander was not at the command at that moment. The operations people wrote it this way for me to sign, because there was already a decision of the corps commander that had been verified by the army commander. So this task had already been defined by the army command vis-a-vis the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're saying between the 13th of August, when General Pavkovic made this remark at the Joint Command meeting, and the 14th of August, when you signed that order, you had no communication from him about your being responsible for this action? Why would he tell -- let me ask you this question: Why would he tell Mr. Stanisic and General Lukic and Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, those persons present at the Joint Command meeting on the 13th of August, why would he go out of the way to make the point that his Chief of Staff was going to have this action under him? He told all those people and he didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Pavkovic said what is written here -- well, you are now asking me to assess this, analyse it, not to say guess. If he told this group of people that an action would be carried out in the border belt, that his Chief of Staff of the corps is in Djakovica, probably he wanted to draw their attention to that, that preparations would be carried out in a timely way through control on my part. I repeat that. I'm just assuming this. Now, what is written here are, are these General Pavkovic's words or not? I am trying to find a logical explanation through my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Me too. What -- what happened with this action? Do you know? Did it take place? On the 15th of August, as -- as envisaged by this decision?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This action did happen. Five police officers got killed, one army officer, and one soldier. And this terrorist stronghold in the border belt was neutralised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you would look at item 6 in this decision, under "Command and communications," the English says: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija with the Pristina Corps forward command post in Djakovica." That's slightly different from some of the other command and communications instructions we've seen. But this one seemed to contemplate the Joint Command with the forward command post, where you were, and you being the person who signed this decision for this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I believe there is possibly a mistake in translation, because according to my understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying the -- the mistake is in the translation of paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask the witness to read paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what I -- that's what I wanted to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read out loud the start of paragraph 6, please, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Combat activities will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you signed this document. At the time, did you notice the words "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" in bold letters a few centimetres above your signature?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I've already explained over the past few days on a few other documents like this too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you -- if you're moving to that rather different issue, can I just be clear about one thing. Anyone reading this document and being told that the operation was commanded from the joint -- from the forward command post in Djakovica - and by "anyone," I mean an inferior officer, a subordinate officer - who would he assume was actually commanding the operation? Or rather, the action. Sorry, my mistake. Commanding the action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over here the actual person is not specified. It's not an individual that is specified. The mainstay of command is the forward command post of the Pristina Corps. With your leave, Your Honour, Mr. President, the previous action, Ratis, Glodjane, has this same qualification that was signed by the corps commander. This has nothing to do with the signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand what your -- I understand your point about this. But I just want to be clear about how far it goes. I'm a -- a subordinate of yours and I get a document that has this paragraph 6 about the command being at the forward command post and it's signed by you and I want to go back for instructions on something. Who would I think was the person I should go to? Standing the overall terms of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The subordinate will call the operations centre of the forward command post in Djakovica to speak to a person, an individual, who is in command or control of the action or to receive information, to talk to the commander if he's there, to talk to the chief of staff, if he is standing in for him. You see, he's going to call the forward command post and its operations centre in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who would he normally expect to be the commander at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be the corps commander. It can be the chief of staff. It can be another leader instead of the chief of staff who got the authority to be in charge of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this document does not tell us who is in charge, in command of the action. You only find that out by making further inquiry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here the document does not speak about that. What it says is that command takes place from the forward command post. And who it is, when he calls he will know. Or if preparation had been carried out before that, then one knows who will command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you actually know who -- who was in command of this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already explained, Your Honour, Mr. President, that the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade whose combat group was the mainstay of active actions was in command of that unit. During that period of time, the forward command post in Djakovica was functioning under the control of a large team from the General Staff and they were following what was going on in the field has much as they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade was in the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was for the most part in the broader area of combat activities. And the forward command post is at a distance of about some 10 kilometres from that particular locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us when he was placed in command of that action? And was it by a written order or an oral order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tendered into evidence the order of this brigade commander. I don't know when, how, but we do have in evidence the order of this commander, of the 15th Armoured Brigade. Now, I don't know what the number is so that we could go back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help on that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Continue, if you wish, Mr. Hannis, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 6D731, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Can we have that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, General, let me ask you this: If the commander of the 15th Brigade is in command of this operation, how would some of these other elements know that? How would -- how would the Battle Group 125-2 know that if all they have is this decision?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps units of the combat group participating in the blockade received a decision on the corps commander's map, which has also been entered into evidence here. Secondly, probably - I say "probably" because it's an entire process - the commander is participating in the implementation of this task were prepared, directly for the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we have on the screen now 6D731. Can you tell me where in there it indicates that the commander of the 15th Brigade is in -- in charge of or commanding this action. From what little I can see on the screen, it looks like he's commanding his subordinate group, BG-15-3, but I don't see that he's commanding BG 125-2 or the other groups listed in P1428. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain what this is about without saying whether you're right or wrong. There was only one combat group engaged in action here according to the decision of the corps command, and that is evident from the previous document in item 2, "Tasks for the units." This combat group was issued a special order by the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade. The other units and combat groups continued to hold the previous positions which they had been holding for ten days or so and where they were encircled. You asked about Combat Group 125-2 and all the following ones. Well, for 15 days those units had not budged from their positions. This is a new combat group which arrived to carry out active activities in this area, and it was given a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there is a translation issue again but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move forward, can we see the end of this document? Now, this is where it's misleading. The question to which Mr. Hannis is seeking an answer is: Where is the document that puts the brigade commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade in command of this action? Is that not your question, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're looking for something that comes from above his level putting him in command. Now, is there such a document, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attempted to explain that it's possible that during the preparation for the task, the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade received - and this is frequently the custom. That's the procedure - the person who is in charge of planning the action is designated. But here in my assessment there was no need to designate him specially, because that was the only unit that was being brought in. That was the unit engaged in action. It was new in that position, while all -- whereas, all the others had already been there for more than a fortnight, for 15 days. That's why this particular unit is being issued with this order for action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have a question about that in 1428. But first, before we leave this one that's on the screen, the last line before the signature says: "All forces during b/d" -- and is that combat operations? Can you explain that acronym for me? What does the "b/d" stand for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all forces in the carrying out of combat activities, the command of the Pristina Corps will be in command of these from the forward command post. The brigade commander copied a sentence from the decision issued by the corps command. He translated it, so to speak, into his own language because for him a Joint Command is not a Joint Command. Rather, it's the command of the Pristina Corps which will be at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if he had received an order placing him in command of this operation, why would he care about whether it was a Joint Command or not? And why is he saying "all forces will be under the command and control of the forward command post of the Pristina Corps Command"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the other units neighbouring to this unit with which he might need to coordinate in combat activities, if he cannot solve this problem directly, he should refer it to the corps command in order to regulate coordination through the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, from some of your earlier answers, I would take it that you, as you're supposing for Colonel Cirkovic, you share the belief that a Joint Command is not a Joint Command. So why in the order you signed, 1428, do we have "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" in bold letters above your name? Why didn't you just leave it out, like you're trying to say he did?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me for a little while and let me try to explain the following: When actions of support and coordinated action between the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia were being conducted, the term "Joint Command" was used to mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, I just asked you a simple question. Why didn't you just leave it out? If you didn't think a Joint Command was a Joint Command, why is that in the order you signed on the 13th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with due respect, I'm trying to respond. I'm trying to reply, if you let me. Because the subordinate units had to be shown that there had to be coordinated action during the execution of the task, coordinated action between the army and the police. That was fundamental, that these were combined coordinated activities with separate chains of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why does that not apply to the document on the screen? Which does involve coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. But this coordinated action was regulated at the corps command and the MUP Staff, and that term was used when addressing subordinates. When it arrived, when the subordinates received it, they would translate it into their own terms and they would know only about the corps command to which they would report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, why didn't you then use what you've insisted earlier was the proper term? Why didn't you say "the combined operations command," instead of "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir -- and may I say directly, I wish it had been so. That would have saved you all this trouble with us. But that is a derived term from the aspect of the Rules of Combat it's an erroneous term. It's combined. Somebody christened it "joint," so here we are. I'm trying to explain to you what this means, how it came into being, where it came from, what it relies on, and what it meant in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, you've told us a few times about "somebody christened it 'the Joint Command'," this non-existent body. Who christened it? You must know. Who came up with that term?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that -- Your Honours, I am being burdened with having to know something. I'm trying to assist, both myself and all of us here in the courtroom. At the forward command post, I saw and received such documents emanating from the corps command, but with the best intentions I really cannot tell you who first christened it this and who first used that term. I saw in the documents - not then, but now - that the army commander and the army Chief of Staff used the term, even Perisic in the General Staff. At the time I really didn't think about this. I wish I had. At least then I would be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, is this the first time that you signed a document that had a reference to "the Joint Command" in it? I know we've got one later in March that you signed.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to 1998, I really don't know. It's possible that there may be other documents, but I really don't know. I'm not saying either that there are or that there aren't. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you've heard me ask this question of some of the other professional soldiers, retired generals, and colonels who have come to testify here, so I'll ask you as well. I mean, as a professional soldier, doesn't the word "command" have a special significance for you, different than what it is for civilians? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you? Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what civilians mean by "command" or who among the civilians uses this term, with what meaning, but I really don't know what civilians mean by "command." I agree with you, of course. But what they mean by "command," I don't know. And I don't know whether I should go on to explain what it means in military terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you -- are you seriously saying that as an ordinary citizen you don't know what people mean when they use the word "command"? You might command your dog to do something or -- you could use the word "command" in all sorts of situations. You say you don't understand what that means in ordinary, everyday language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't thought about it, Your Honour. I'm referring to "command" in the military sense of the word. What does "military command" mean? At what level? And if that's what you're asking me, I'm really willing to try and respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Hannis wants to know. He wants the definition of "command" in military circles. He wants to know whether it's got special significance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly it has a concrete meaning. "Command" is an organisational part of the Army of Yugoslavia which has its establishment, its organisation, its composition, its structure, its purpose, its tasks, its powers; furthermore, it has its location, it has buildings, premises, and internal communications and relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to get at, General, is that in an organisation in the military, in the army, "command" is a very important term; "chain of command" is a very important concept. And from my brief experience in my army, there was a big difference when I heard the words "command" or "chain of command" when I was in the army, as opposed to when I might hear it out in my prosecutor's office. So if I were in the army and I were a commander and I saw some document making reference to "the Joint Command," my curiosity would be piqued. I would want to know: Well, who in the heck is this Joint Command and what are they trying to do suggesting something or proposing something or commanding some of my subordinates? I would be at least motivated to investigate. Did you do that? The first time you saw this term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," did you try to find out who it was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw this term in a document, and bearing in mind the content of that particular document - I don't recall which was actually the first one - but it defined relations of cooperation between the army and the police in the carrying out of a certain combat task. So I understood this term to refer to the plan of coordination between these two structures and the possibility in a certain part of the implementation of the task to have combined command so that in one location you would find a representative of the army and a representative of the police monitoring the situation for a certain period of time, each of them commanding his own units. I understood it to be a synonym for "combined command" and "combined command post."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That seems to be -- that seems to be inconsistent with what I heard you say before about the difference between a combined command post and a joint command post. I thought your point was that a joint command post suggested one chain of command for two different structures or unit from -- from a different organisation. Is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a reference. Where did General Lazarevic say this? Where? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I can get a reference if the general needs it, but I don't think he needs a reference to explain the difference. If I'm wrong, he can tell me I'm wrong. If he didn't say that, he can say he doesn't recall saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's being asserted, as I understand it, Mr. Hannis, that this is wrong, this recollection of yours. So what sort, what is a source for it. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, right at the end of the day I asked him this exact question, describe for us what this joint post was. Who was there. What it was like. He gave exactly this answer, almost world for word. So it's not that he said something different before, he said exactly the same way before. It was a place where they could coordinate together, each commanding its own forces, MUP and VJ. Same thing he said yesterday. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll withdraw this question for now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you can deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My recollection is consistent with yours, Mr. Hannis. And it may be there's two different concepts of command, there's command and command post and there are different descriptions. You check that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we look at the document that we just had on the screen - I think it's maybe still there - it's paragraph 7, the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the very top, you see a description of a command post located in the Cesta feature. That's the command post that this commander is going to operate those troops from. That's a different thing from the command post at the forward command of the Pristina Corps. And it's important that those differences are understood. You can't -- you can't mix apples and oranges when you're talking about the command of a military action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is withdrawn, and it can be revived if Mr. Hannis can find a proper foundation for it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me follow up on what Mr. Ackerman just said. We're looking at that 6D document on the screen, 6D731. This is Colonel Cirkovic saying the command post is in the general area of the Cesta feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suggest to you, General, that that means his command post for the elements of the 15th Armoured Brigade is in the area of the Cesta feature, but the overall command post for all the forces engaged in this operation -- or this action in P14 -- 1428, is at the Pristina Corps forward command post. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read it out correctly, the first part and the second part, and I gave the answer I gave; and I never claimed that a Joint Command is a single chain of command. I never asserted that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And you said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said in an earlier answer explaining why it was your position that Colonel Cirkovic was in command of this operation was because it was only elements of the 15th that were actually doing anything; everybody else was just holding positions. In 1428, item 2.2, it says: "Battle Group -- BG 125-2 is to carry out a diversionary attack." So the 125th is doing something as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This combat group from the composition of the 125th Brigade, not battalion, is carrying out a demonstration attack. It's not really attacking. They're on the move. And I know that indeed from that period of time they were in the area for already 15 days. The command of the brigade did not give any particular task in writing to this combat group. They moved in a given direction 500 metres and then went back, because they were under blockade for 15 days already. That's the way it was with the other groups too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean the command of the 15th did not give any command to the 125th; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am sorry. Please take a look at the order. Please. Let us all together look at the order of the brigade commander. I am saying this from my own memory, and also you'll see it in writing. We can take it back to the screen too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're in this very difficult position again of having to interrupt. We have no option, Mr. Hannis. Apparently it takes a full half hour for technology to be rewound for the next trial. So we shall have to adjourn at this stage and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
